clue.text: Fed up with money leaving, putting the squeeze on education

indicators.note: the two outer pieces press in on either side of the education piece, holding it between them

parts.note: brass is British slang for money
off means departing, as in 'I'm off'

explanation.surface: Someone resents money disappearing while education budgets are squeezed.
explanation.walkthrough: Brass is British slang for money, and the answer is British slang for annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being fed up and being brassed off are both informal ways of saying thoroughly annoyed.

clue.text: Betray Cosa Nostra, having ripped off leader's liqueur

parts.note: to rat on someone is to betray them

indicators.note: the leading letter of the gang's name is torn away

parts.note: the Cosa Nostra is the Sicilian Mafia

explanation.surface: An informer betrays the Mob after its boss has been robbed, all over a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ripped off' sounds like the Mafia being swindled; here it strips the first letter, M, leaving AFIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratafia is an almond- or fruit-flavoured sweet liqueur.

clue.text: Usual chaos of university supporters getting upset

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the letters read from the bottom up

parts.note: fans are supporters of a team

explanation.surface: Students' football supporters riot in the habitual mayhem.
explanation.walkthrough: U plus FANS gives UFANS; 'getting upset' reverses it upward.
explanation.definitionFit: SNAFU is military slang, 'situation normal: all fouled up', the routine mess everyone expects.

clue.text: Lens used to observe ocular prosthesis having exchanged components

indicators.note: the two halves of the two-word phrase swap places

parts.note: a glass eye is an artificial eye

explanation.surface: A lens is fitted to an artificial eye with its parts swapped round.
explanation.walkthrough: GLASS EYE with its two words exchanged gives EYE GLASS.
explanation.definitionFit: A monocle-style eyeglass is a single lens held to one eye for seeing better.

clue.text: Brilliant teacher turned up on time, which attracts interest

parts.note: brilliant work is outstanding

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the letters are read from the bottom upward

parts.note: a BEd (Bachelor of Education) is a teacher's degree, standing for a teacher

explanation.surface: A brilliant teacher arrived punctually, and that draws everyone's attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' looks like arriving; it reverses BED to DEB. 'which attracts interest' stands for 'a thing which attracts interest'.
explanation.definitionFit: An unpaid loan keeps accruing interest charges, a financial rather than an attentive kind of interest.

clue.text: Grand Prix race track in Berkshire unfinished? What a debacle!

parts.note: F1 (Formula One) is Grand Prix racing, with the 1 read as the letter I

indicators.note: the racecourse's name loses its final letter

parts.note: Ascot is a racecourse in Berkshire

explanation.surface: A motor race staged at a half-built Berkshire course would be a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: F1 is written FI. ASCOT is a famous horse-racing course in Berkshire, an English county; 'unfinished' drops its T.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiasco is a humiliating failure, the same as a debacle.

clue.text: American wife over 50 having done a runner?

parts.note: O is the cricket abbreviation for over
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: An American wife over fifty has run off.
explanation.definitionFit: AWOL, absent without leave, describes someone who has fled; 'done a runner' is British slang for running off.

clue.text: Might oral be getting reviewed because of this?

definitions.text: Might oral be getting reviewed because of this?

indicators.note: to review is to go over again and revise, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: An exam board wonders whether a spoken test might be re-marked by a computer procedure.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearranging MIGHT ORAL gives the answer, and the whole clue describes it: automated marking can trigger reviews.
explanation.definitionFit: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure, like those used to grade or moderate exam results.

clue.text: Error that hurt Logan, unfortunately

parts.note: ow is the cry of someone hurt

indicators.note: something gone wrong suggests the letters have gone wrong too, so they are reordered

explanation.surface: A footballer called Logan suffers a painful blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: OW (the cry when hurt) plus NGOAL, a rearrangement of LOGAN from 'unfortunately'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoring into your own net is the classic footballing error, and by extension any self-inflicted blunder.

clue.text: Italian hot-head rejecting opening stake

indicators.note: rejecting sends the word back, so it is read from right to left

parts.note: the ante is the stake put in before a poker hand opens

explanation.surface: A fiery Italian refuses to put up the opening stake at cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hot-head' looks like a temperamental person; it is a volcano's fiery summit.
explanation.definitionFit: Etna is the active volcano on Sicily, a mountain with a molten top.

clue.text: Cutting ties with European throttling missing pupil

indicators.note: the word for throttling lacks the letter for a learner

parts.note: throttling someone is strangling them
L is a learner, from the L-plate on a learner driver's car

explanation.surface: A European chokes a truant student, ending their relationship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing' drops L from STRANGLING.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange someone is to alienate them, breaking the bond between you.

clue.text: Bombproof quality insulating regulator

indicators.note: the outer words wrap round and enclose the letters needed, as insulation surrounds a wire

explanation.surface: A bombproof standard of material insulates the watchdog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'insulating' picks out OFQUAL from inside BombprOOF QUALity.
explanation.definitionFit: Ofqual is the government body overseeing exams and qualifications in England.

clue.text: Nail to secure back bit of stable

parts.note: a tack is a small nail

indicators.note: back tells us the word for securing a boat is read in reverse

parts.note: to moor a boat is to secure it

explanation.surface: Instructions to nail down the back section of a stable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses MOOR to ROOM.
explanation.definitionFit: A tack room holds saddles and bridles and is part of a stable block.

clue.text: Exploits cricket's principal trophy when batting

indicators.note: the principal letter is the leading one of the word

parts.note: the Ashes is the trophy contested in England-Australia Test cricket
in cricket the side batting is said to be in

explanation.surface: A cricket writer's notes on the game's top prize while the side is batting.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ashes is the urn played for in England v Australia Test cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: To cash in on something is to profit from it, to take advantage of it.

clue.text: Novel Dahl wrote to stand up to examination

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Roald Dahl wrote a novel that survives critical scrutiny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a noun for a book; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An argument that holds water is sound and survives testing, like a vessel without leaks.

clue.text: High temperature? Totally

parts.note: all means totally, as in 'all alone'; that the same letters also sit inside the word is a coincidence

explanation.surface: A high temperature? Completely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High temperature' reads as one phrase, but 'High' is the definition and 'temperature' gives T.
explanation.definitionFit: Tall and high both describe something of great height.

clue.text: Quiet stroll on small street in York

parts.note: sh is a call for quiet
to amble is to stroll

explanation.surface: A hushed walk along a little street in York.
explanation.walkthrough: The Shambles is a famous medieval street in York, in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: York's Shambles is a narrow historic street, named after the old meat stalls once there.

clue.text: Feasible, occasionally, to come up short

indicators.note: occasionally means every so often, so every other letter is taken

explanation.surface: A plan is sometimes possible yet still falls short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'occasionally' takes F, A, I, L from Feasible.
explanation.definitionFit: To fail is not to meet a standard or target.

clue.text: Five English large beers outside? A challenge for 18 year-olds!

definitions.note: singular in the clue but the answer is the plural set of exams, taken together as one challenge

indicators.note: the beer word goes round the outside of the three single letters

parts.note: ales are beers
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: Five large English beers: a test for teenagers just old enough to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: '18' is not a cross-reference here, just an age. A levels are the exams English school-leavers sit at about eighteen.
explanation.definitionFit: A levels are the final school exams in England, taken at around age eighteen.

clue.text: Drone — boring, senseless, cruel

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so the drone word goes inside

parts.note: inane means senseless or silly
a drone is a low hum

explanation.surface: A dull, mindless speaker is unkind as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' looks like a synonym for dull, joining the list of insults; it means drilling into.
explanation.definitionFit: Inhumane means lacking compassion, the same as cruel.

clue.text: I gather Bevan tasted chemical compound

indicators.note: I gather means I hear, so the words are judged by how they sound

parts.note: Nye Bevan was the Labour politician who founded the NHS; tasted means tried

explanation.surface: Rumour has it a famous politician sampled a chemical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I gather' looks like hearsay; it signals a sound-alike. NYE TRIED is said like the answer. Aneurin 'Nye' Bevan was a British Labour minister.
explanation.definitionFit: A nitride is a compound of nitrogen with another element, such as boron or silicon.

clue.text: Terrible mistake getting into flipping cheap UK cocaine

indicators.note: flipping says the hidden letters are read backwards
getting into means going inside the words, where the needed letters lie concealed

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Getting involved with cheap British cocaine would be a dreadful error.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft put 'getting into' in the definition, but it is the indicator for letters inside cheaP UK COCaine; 'flipping' turns PUKCOC round.
explanation.definitionFit: A cock-up is British slang for a botched job or serious blunder.

clue.text: ERG: nowt affected Gavin's first blunder

indicators.note: affected means altered, so these letters are changed in order
first takes the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: A physics note: one unit of work achieved nothing, and Gavin's first attempt was a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affected' rearranges ERG and NOWT to GETWRON; Gavin's first letter, G, ends it. Nowt is northern English for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: To get something wrong is to make an error over it, to blunder.

clue.text: Doctor, last month, son loses hair

parts.note: MO is a medical officer, a doctor
ult, short for ultimo, means of last month in old business letters

explanation.surface: A doctor reports that a son started going bald a month ago.
explanation.walkthrough: ULT (ultimo) is old commercial shorthand for last month.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal that moults sheds its fur or feathers.

clue.text: U-boat evacuated vessel making a sudden change of course

indicators.note: evacuated means emptied, so only the outside letters remain

parts.note: an urn is a vessel

explanation.surface: An abandoned submarine abruptly swings round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'evacuated' empties U-boat to UT.
explanation.definitionFit: A U-turn is a complete reversal of direction, literally or of policy.

clue.text: The King enters: "Let Handel composition be the last notes I'll hear"

indicators.note: the single letter goes into the middle of the rearranged letters
a composition is something put together, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dying monarch asks for a Handel piece as his final music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composition' looks musical; it rearranges LET HANDEL to DEATHNELL, and K 'enters' it.
explanation.definitionFit: A death knell is the bell tolled at a death, the final sound heralding the end.

clue.text: One upper-class idiot

parts.note: nit is British slang for an idiot

explanation.surface: A single toff who is a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is a single thing, the number one.

clue.text: Sailor transporting Saint Nicholas to Russia?

indicators.note: the sailor carries the saint's letter inside him

parts.note: a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor ferries Saint Nicholas to Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saint Nicholas' reads as one name; split, Saint gives S and Nicholas belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas II was the last Russian emperor, the Romanov monarch overthrown in 1917.

clue.text: Unhappily, Ant pursued intention to divorce

indicators.note: unhappy letters are disturbed, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Ant, sadly, followed through on plans to split up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unhappily' rearranges ANT PURSUED.
explanation.definitionFit: To put asunder is to separate, as in the wedding service, 'let no man put asunder'.
